title: US westward expansion and Native American dispossession
summary: With the Louisiana Purchase of 1803 the United States doubled its size, buying 828,000 square miles west of the Mississippi from France. Settlers pushing west saw Native nations as the obstacle. The government used war, treaties and the Removal Act of 1830 to move eastern peoples beyond the Mississippi, nearly 50,000 of them to Indian Territory, at times breaking treaties and defying the Supreme Court; Cherokee removal became the Trail of Tears. The Dawes Act of 1887 then broke reservations into individual allotments.

uncertainty.note: Spans from the Louisiana Purchase in 1803 to the culmination of the Plains Wars and the demographic closing of the frontier around 1890.

as_recorded.value: In this transaction with France, signed on April 30, 1803, the United States purchased 828,000 square miles of land west of the Mississippi River for $15 million
The U.S. Government used treaties as one means to displace Indians from their tribal lands, a mechanism that was strengthened with the Removal Act of 1830
Approved on February 8, 1887, "An Act to Provide for the Allotment of Lands in Severalty to Indians on the Various Reservations," known as the Dawes Act

importance.justification: Doubled US territory and stripped Native nations of most of their lands east and west of the Mississippi (R3 D3 T3 L3).

audience_note: Describes the forced removal and dispossession of Native American nations.

related.because: American independence established a sovereign republic whose federal and state policies drove westward settlement into Indigenous lands.
Colonial settlement patterns and treaties established the precedent of seizing Indigenous territories for Euro-American settlers.
